config.title: Write a throttle utility

intro.title: Write a throttle utility
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a throttle utility function in JavaScript. A throttle function limits how often a given function can be executed over time, which is useful for optimizing performance in scenarios like handling rapid user input or scroll events. You will learn the core programming concept of controlling function execution timing using timers and closures. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, the setTimeout API, and managing state within a closure. By the end, you'll have a reusable throttle utility that can help make your applications more efficient.
intro.usecase: Throttling is essential for optimizing performance in interactive web applications where frequent events can overwhelm systems. In dashboard interfaces with real-time data visualizations, throttling prevents excessive API calls when users rapidly adjust date range sliders or filter controls. Search input fields use throttling to delay search execution until users pause typing, reducing unnecessary network requests. Similarly, infinite scroll implementations throttle scroll events to load content batches efficiently without janky scrolling experiences.

objectives: Implement a throttle function that limits the execution rate of another function
Configure the throttle delay parameter to control the minimum time between function calls
Initialize and manage a timer variable to track when the next function execution is allowed
Apply the throttle utility to event handlers to prevent excessive UI updates
Construct a demonstration that visually shows throttled versus unthrottled event firing
Manipulate the throttle delay during runtime to observe different throttling behaviors
Integrate the throttle utility with common DOM events like scroll, resize, or mousemove

steps.title: Create a basic function to be throttled
steps.instruction: Create a simple function named logMessage that logs 'Button clicked!' to the console.
steps.hint: Define a function using either function declaration or arrow function syntax that calls console.log() with the message.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a function that can be called to log a message, which we'll later throttle.
successCriteria: A function named logMessage exists and logs 'Button clicked!' when called.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named exactly 'logMessage' and logs the exact message 'Button clicked!'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function called logMessage that logs 'Button clicked!' to the console.

steps.title: Create the throttle function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'throttle' that takes two parameters: 'callback' and 'delay'.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts two arguments. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.

steps.expectedOutcome: A throttle function skeleton with the correct parameters is created.
successCriteria: The code defines a function named 'throttle' that accepts 'callback' and 'delay' as parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function is named 'throttle' and accepts both 'callback' and 'delay' as parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle function isn't properly defined. Create a function named 'throttle' that takes 'callback' and 'delay' as parameters.

steps.title: Add last execution time tracking
steps.instruction: Inside your throttle function, add a variable named 'lastExecuted' to track when the function was last called. Initialize it to 0.
steps.hint: Create a variable using 'let' or 'const' inside the throttle function. Since we need to track time, we'll use a number (0 means never executed).
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function now has a variable to track the last execution time.
successCriteria: The throttle function contains a variable named 'lastExecuted' initialized to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a variable named 'lastExecuted' and initialized it to 0 inside the throttle function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle function should have a variable named 'lastExecuted' set to 0 to track when the function was last called.

steps.title: Add timeout reference storage
steps.instruction: Inside the throttle function, add a variable to store the timeout ID for delayed execution. Initialize it as null.
steps.hint: You'll need to declare a variable (like timeoutId) that can hold the timeout reference returned by setTimeout.
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function now has a variable to track the timeout ID, which will be used to manage delayed executions.
successCriteria: A variable (e.g., timeoutId) is declared inside the throttle function and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you declare the variable inside the throttle function and initialize it to null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle function needs a variable to store timeout IDs. Try adding something like 'let timeoutId = null;' inside the function.

steps.title: Implement the throttled function logic
steps.instruction: Inside the throttle function, return a new function that will implement the throttling behavior.
steps.hint: The returned function should accept arguments and contain the throttling logic.
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function now returns another function that will later contain the throttling logic.
successCriteria: The throttle function returns a function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure throttle returns a function (it can be an arrow or regular function).
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle function should return a new function. Try adding `return function(...args) { }` or `return (...args) => { }` inside throttle.

steps.title: Add immediate execution logic
steps.instruction: Inside the throttle function, add logic to execute the provided function immediately if enough time has passed since the last execution.
steps.hint: Check if the current time minus the last executed time is greater than or equal to the delay. If true, execute the function and update the last executed time.
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function now includes logic to execute the callback immediately when enough time has passed since the last execution.
successCriteria: The throttle function checks if enough time has passed and executes the callback immediately, updating the last executed time.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're checking if enough time has passed and executing the function immediately when true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The immediate execution logic isn't quite right. Review the example and try again.

steps.title: Add delayed execution logic
steps.instruction: Inside the returned function of your throttle function, add logic to schedule the callback for later execution using setTimeout when immediate execution is not allowed.
steps.hint: Use setTimeout to call the original function after the delay has passed. Store the timeout ID in the timeout variable you already declared.
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function will now properly schedule delayed executions when the function is called too frequently.
successCriteria: The throttle function includes setTimeout logic inside the returned function to schedule delayed execution.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you've properly implemented the setTimeout logic inside the returned function. Make sure you're storing the timeout ID and calling the original function with the correct arguments.
steps.feedbackWrong: The delayed execution logic isn't quite right. Look at the analogous example for how setTimeout works, and make sure you're implementing it inside the returned function of your throttle function.

steps.title: Test the throttle function with a button
steps.instruction: Create a button element that calls the throttled function when clicked.
steps.hint: Add a button with an onClick handler that calls the throttled function.

<button onClick={() => console.log('Clicked!')}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element that triggers the throttled function when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element with an onClick handler that calls the throttled function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the button has an onClick handler that calls the throttled function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a button element with an onClick handler that calls the throttled function.

steps.title: Add visual feedback for function calls
steps.instruction: Create a variable to track the number of times the throttled function has been called, and display this count in the console when the function executes.
steps.hint: Initialize a counter variable inside the throttle function, increment it when the original function is called, and log the current count.
steps.expectedOutcome: The throttle function will now track and display how many times it has executed the original function, providing visual feedback of the throttling behavior.
successCriteria: The throttle function includes a call counter that increments and logs to the console each time the original function executes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to both increment the counter and log the current count when the function executes.
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle function doesn't yet track or display call counts. Add a counter variable and log it when the function executes.

steps.title: Test the throttle with rapid clicks
steps.instruction: Click the button rapidly to observe how the throttle function limits execution to once per second.
steps.hint: Click the button multiple times quickly and watch the console output or visual feedback to see that executions are throttled.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see that rapid clicks only trigger the throttled function once per second, demonstrating the throttle utility in action.
successCriteria: The throttle function correctly limits execution frequency when the button is clicked rapidly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to click the button rapidly and observe the execution pattern matches throttle behavior.
steps.feedbackWrong: The throttle isn't working as expected. Review the throttle implementation and test again with rapid clicks.
